Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 17
Let G be a directed graph. Define the transitive closure GT as the directed graph sharing
the same vertex set as G, where an edge u →v exists in GT if and only if there is a
directed path from u to v in G. Furthermore, define a transitive reduction of G to be a
graph with the minimum number of edges such that its transitive closure is identical to
GT. Given that a graph may generally admit multiple transitive reductions, prove that
G possesses a unique transitive reduction if and only if G is acyclic.

0004 | there is a directed path from u to v in G. Furthermore, define a transitive reduction of G to

0006 | GT. Given that a graph may generally admit multiple transitive reductions, prove that G
0007 | possesses a unique transitive reduction if and only if G is acyclic.
0008 | Theorem 1. Let G be a directed graph. Then G possesses a unique transitive reduction if
0009 | and only if G is acyclic.
0010 | Proof. We prove both directions of the equivalence.
0011 | (⇒) If G is acyclic, then G has a unique transitive reduction.
0012 | Assume G is acyclic. Since G is acyclic, its transitive closure GT is also acyclic (as paths
0013 | in G cannot create cycles).
0014 | Define the relation:
0015 | R = {(u, v) ∈GT : ∄w ̸= u, v such that (u, w) ∈GT and (w, v) ∈GT}
0016 | (1)
0017 | That is, R consists of all edges in GT that cannot be obtained by composing two other
0018 | edges via transitivity.
0019 | Lemma 1. The graph R defined above satisfies RT = GT.
0020 | Proof of Lemma. Since R ⊆GT by construction, we have RT ⊆GT.
0021 | For the reverse inclusion, let (u, v) ∈GT. We prove (u, v) ∈RT by strong induction on
0022 | the length of the shortest path from u to v in G.
0023 | Base case: If the shortest path has length 1, then (u, v) is a direct edge in G, hence in
0024 | GT. Moreover, there is no intermediate vertex w with paths u →w →v, so (u, v) ∈R, and
0025 | thus (u, v) ∈RT.
0026 | Inductive step: Suppose the shortest path from u to v in G has length k > 1. If (u, v) ∈R,
0027 | we are done. Otherwise, there exists w ̸= u, v with (u, w), (w, v) ∈GT. The shortest paths
0028 | from u to w and from w to v have lengths strictly less than k (since G is acyclic). By the
0029 | inductive hypothesis, (u, w), (w, v) ∈RT. Therefore, (u, v) ∈RT by transitivity.
0030 | Lemma 2. R has the minimum number of edges among all graphs with transitive closure
0031 | GT.
0032 | Proof of Lemma. Suppose R′ is any graph with R′T = GT. We show |R′| ≥|R|.
0033 | For any (u, v) ∈R, by definition there is no intermediate vertex w such that (u, w), (w, v) ∈
0034 | GT. This means any path from u to v in GT must include the direct edge (u, v).
0035 | Since R′T = GT, there must be a path from u to v in R′. If (u, v) /∈R′, then this path
0036 | must go through some intermediate vertex w′ with (u, w′) ∈R′T and (w′, v) ∈R′T. But
0037 | since R′T = GT, we have (u, w′), (w′, v) ∈GT, contradicting the definition of (u, v) ∈R.
0038 | Therefore, (u, v) ∈R′ for all (u, v) ∈R, which implies |R′| ≥|R|.
0039 | Lemma 3. R is the unique transitive reduction.
